steps.example:
# This is a note for people
print("Hi")  # this part is ignored too
steps.text:
A line that starts with `#` is a **comment**. Python ignores it. Comments are notes for the people who read your code.

A `#` can also come after some code. Python ignores everything from the `#` to the end of the line.

Everyone gets errors, even experts. An error is not a failure. It is Python telling you that it didn't understand something.

When there is an error, the program stops. The message tells you **which line** has the problem and **what kind** of problem it is. Read it, fix the line and run again.

A **program** is a list of instructions for a computer. The computer follows them exactly, one after another.

In Python, `print` is an instruction that shows a message on the screen. The message goes inside the round brackets, in quotes.

The box with code in it is the **editor**. You can type in it.

Press **Run** to see what your program does. You can run it as often as you like.

When an exercise has a **Check** button, press it when you are done. Check runs your program and tells you if it does what the exercise asks.

Python runs a program from the **top** line to the **bottom** line, one line at a time. It never skips ahead.

So the order of the lines is the order of what you see.

`print` shows what you put inside its round brackets. Text goes in quotes. Every `print` starts on a new line.

With nothing inside the brackets, `print()` shows an empty line.

steps.example:
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")
print("no new line", end="!")
print()
steps.text:
`print` puts a space between values and starts a new line at the end. You can change both:

- `sep=` sets what goes **between** the values.
- `end=` sets what comes **after** the last value.

`print` can show several values. Separate them with commas, and `print` puts a space between them.

The `+` sign is different. It glues two strings together with **no** space.

Time for a small project! You will print a business card, step by step.

Use what you know: `print`, strings, new lines, `sep=` and `end=`.

Python can do sums. `2 + 3` is an **expression**: Python works out its value, `5`, before `print` shows it.

In quotes, `"2 + 3"` is just text, so Python shows it as it is. You will learn much more about numbers later.

steps.example_output:
Line one
Line two
Name:	Ada
steps.text:
A backslash `\` inside a string starts a special character:

- `\n` starts a new line.
- `\t` adds a tab, a wide space.
- `\"` and `\'` are quotes that don't end the text.
- `\\` is one backslash.

Text in Python is called a **string**. A string goes inside quotes: `"Hello"` or `'Hello'`. Both kinds work, but the start and the end must match.

Without quotes, Python thinks a word is the name of something. Then it shows an error.
Watch out for curly quotes like “this”. Phones and word processors often add them. Python only understands straight quotes: `"` and `'`.

What if the text itself has a quote in it, like `It's`? Put the other kind of quote around it:

- `"It's sunny"` has a `'` inside, so it uses `"` around it.
- `'She said "hi"'` has a `"` inside, so it uses `'` around it.

If the quote inside is the same kind as the ones around it, Python thinks the text ends there.

A **variable** is a name that stores a value. This line makes a variable called `city` and stores `"Paris"` in it:

    city = "Paris"

The `=` means "store". The name always goes on the **left**, and the value goes on the right.

A **NameError** means Python doesn't know a name. There are three usual reasons:

- a typing mistake, like `nmae` instead of `name`
- missing quotes around some text
- using a variable before the line that gives it a value

The error shows the name and the line. Check those first.

You choose the names of your variables, but there are rules:

- Use letters, digits and `_`. No spaces.
- Don't start with a digit.
- Capital letters matter: `name` and `Name` are different.
- Don't use names Python already uses, like `print`.

Good names say what the value is, like `first_name`.

A variable can get a new value later in the program. The old value is gone: the variable only
remembers the **latest** value it was given.

lessons.title: Giving a variable a new value

steps.example:
a = "left"
b = "right"
temp = a
a = b
b = temp
print(a, b)
steps.text:
To swap the values of `a` and `b`, you might write `a = b` and then `b = a`. But after `a = b`, the old value of `a` is gone!

The fix is a third variable that keeps a copy first:

    temp = a
    a = b
    b = temp

steps.example:
a = "red"
b = a
a = "blue"
print(a, b)
steps.text:
To understand a program, **trace** it. Go through it line by line, like Python does, and keep track of the current value of each variable. When a variable gets a new value, cross out the old one.

A variable holds a **value**, not a link to another variable. `b = a` copies the value that `a` has right now.

When Python sees a variable's name in your code, it uses the **value** stored in that variable.
Words inside quotes are just text, so `"name"` and `name` mean different things.
